explanation.summary: Postpartum contraception considers VTE risk (elevated for 6 weeks), lactation and future spacing. Progestogen-only methods (mini-pill, subdermal implant, depot, or hormonal IUD) are safe in breastfeeding and do not reduce milk supply. Combined hormonal methods are generally deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum, and longer if VTE risk factors are present or milk supply is not established. Long-acting reversible contraception (implant or IUS) is preferred where possible for spacing preference. IUD insertion is either within 48 hours of birth or after 4 weeks.
key_points: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum.
Progestogen-only methods are safe in lactation and do not reduce milk supply.
IUD insertion is either within 48 hours or after 4 weeks postpartum.
LAM is only reliable under 6 months with full breastfeeding and amenorrhoea.
explanation.pearls: At 4 weeks postpartum in a breastfeeding woman with negative bhCG, an etonogestrel implant is immediately effective and does not affect milk supply; combined pills are deferred until at least 6 weeks.

options.rationale: DMPA is progestogen-only but reduces bone density over years of use; an implant or IUS is preferred long-acting choice here. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

Copper IUD is a good option but the 4 week postpartum window still risks expulsion; the standard IUD insertion window is either within 48 hours or after 4 weeks with cervical assessment. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

LAM is only reliable when all three criteria (fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, under 6 months) apply and she wants active contraception now. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum for VTE risk and can reduce milk supply while lactation is being established. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

Progestogen-only implant is safe in breastfeeding, does not affect milk supply, and provides immediate contraception when inserted before 21 days postpartum or with LAM criteria met. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ and RANZCOG guidance for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP 160/110 or above) recommends oral labetalol, oral immediate-release nifedipine, or IV hydralazine as first-line antihypertensives; all three lower BP predictably in the pregnant patient. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading with 1 g/hour maintenance is added for seizure prophylaxis when the diagnosis is severe pre-eclampsia. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and atenolol are avoided in pregnancy. The target is BP below 160/110 with attention to the risk of causing fetal distress if the drop is precipitous.
key_points: First-line antihypertensives are oral labetalol, oral nifedipine, or IV hydralazine.
Sublingual nifedipine risks abrupt hypotension and is not used.
Magnesium is added for seizure prophylaxis, not as an antihypertensive.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs and atenolol are avoided in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: For a BP of 168/112 in pregnancy give oral labetalol 200 mg (or oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release) and add magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; avoid sublingual nifedipine and ACE inhibitors.

options.rationale: SOMANZ and RANZCOG list oral labetalol as an acceptable first-line agent for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy alongside oral nifedipine and IV hydralazine. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)
Atenolol is associated with fetal growth restriction and is not first-line in acute severe hypertension in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

Magnesium is indicated for seizure prophylaxis with severe pre-eclampsia and is added; it is not itself a BP-lowering agent and should not delay antihypertensive therapy. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)
Sublingual nifedipine can cause abrupt hypotension and fetal distress; oral immediate-release is the AU recommendation with careful monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)
ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy due to renal teratogenicity and are not used to treat pregnancy hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is managed with a standardised RANZCOG algorithm summarised by the HELPERR mnemonic: call for Help, evaluate for Episiotomy (only if needed to access), Legs (McRoberts) with suprapubic Pressure, then internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, reverse Woods, or delivery of the posterior arm), then Roll to all fours. Zavanelli, symphysiotomy or deliberate clavicular fracture is used only when all standard manoeuvres fail. Fundal pressure is contraindicated because it worsens shoulder impaction and increases risks of brachial plexus injury and uterine rupture. Time to delivery of the shoulders correlates with hypoxic injury risk; the whole sequence generally aims to complete within 5 to 7 minutes.
key_points: McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are first-line and resolve 40 to 60 percent.
Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
Internal manoeuvres and all-fours follow if first-line fails.
Zavanelli, symphysiotomy or clavicular fracture is last resort.
explanation.pearls: For shoulder dystocia the first manoeuvre after calling for help is McRoberts with suprapubic pressure; fundal pressure is contraindicated because it worsens the impaction.

options.rationale: Episiotomy is considered when it improves internal manoeuvre access, not as a routine first step; the impaction is a bony problem. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)
RANZCOG algorithm places McRoberts and suprapubic pressure as the first manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia; it resolves 40 to 60 percent of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)
Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia as it worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)
Zavanelli is a last resort after all first- and second-line manoeuvres have failed; it is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)
Symphysiotomy or deliberate clavicular fracture is reserved for failure of internal manoeuvres and all-fours position. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)

explanation.summary: Preterm labour management from 24 to 34 weeks aims to buy 48 hours for antenatal corticosteroids (IM betamethasone 11.4 mg two doses 24 hours apart) and to transfer in utero to a facility with appropriate neonatal care. First-line tocolysis in Australia is oral nifedipine; atosiban is second-line where available. Beta-agonists (salbutamol) are avoided due to maternal cardiovascular risk. Indometacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios. Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when birth is anticipated before 30 weeks (some units extend to 32 weeks).
key_points: Nifedipine oral is first-line tocolytic at 24 to 34 weeks in Australia.
Indometacin is avoided after 32 weeks for ductal closure risk.
Beta-agonists are avoided for maternal cardiovascular safety.
Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection below 30 weeks (some units to 32 weeks).
explanation.pearls: At 32 weeks in preterm labour give oral nifedipine tocolysis with concurrent IM betamethasone; avoid indometacin (ductal closure) and beta-agonists (cardiovascular risk).

options.rationale: Indometacin risks premature ductal closure and oligohydramnios after 32 weeks; nifedipine is preferred at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)
Delay of 48 hours for corticosteroid maturation is beneficial at 32 weeks; tocolysis should be attempted concurrently with steroids. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

RANZCOG and Australian obstetric protocols use oral nifedipine as first-line tocolytic at 24 to 34 weeks because of maternal tolerability and evidence for 48 hour delay allowing corticosteroids. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)
Beta-agonist tocolytics carry unacceptable maternal cardiovascular risk and are second- or third-line only. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)
Atosiban is effective but more costly and less accessible than nifedipine; it is second-line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG recommends offering external cephalic version from 37 weeks in women with singleton term breech and no contraindications (previous caesarean scar being a relative contraindication, plus antepartum haemorrhage, placenta praevia, oligohydramnios, fetal abnormality, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy). ECV is done in a facility with immediate access to caesarean, with tocolysis (typically nifedipine or salbutamol) and continuous CTG. Success rates are 50 to 60 percent in multiparous women and 30 to 40 percent in nulliparous women. Anti-D is given to Rh-negative women within 72 hours of ECV. Vaginal breech delivery is offered only when strict RANZCOG criteria are met with experienced practitioners.
key_points: ECV is first-line for term breech in eligible women.
Performed from 37 weeks with tocolysis and CTG in a birth-ready setting.
Anti-D within 72 hours in Rh-negative women.
Vaginal breech delivery has strict operator and criteria requirements.
explanation.pearls: For a G2P1 with singleton frank breech at 36+2 weeks and no contraindications, offer ECV at 37 weeks with tocolysis and CTG monitoring; anti-D within 72 hours if Rh negative.

options.rationale: Vaginal breech is only offered in selected women with strict criteria and experienced operator; ECV is offered first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)
Moxibustion has limited evidence and is not a substitute for offering ECV in a formal maternity setting. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

ECV should be performed from 37 weeks in a facility with capacity for immediate caesarean if needed and with CTG monitoring; earlier attempts have higher spontaneous version rates that make procedure unnecessary. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)
RANZCOG recommends ECV from 37 weeks in eligible women with singleton term breech to reduce caesarean rate; her situation has no contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)
ECV should be offered first in eligible women because a successful version returns her to routine cephalic vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is a category-1 obstetric emergency requiring delivery within 30 minutes (target 15 to 20). The immediate holding measures are: (1) manually elevate the presenting part with two fingers in the vagina to relieve cord compression, keep the fingers in place during transfer if possible; (2) position the mother in knee-chest, exaggerated Sims or Trendelenburg; (3) fill the bladder with 500 mL warmed saline via Foley catheter (raises the presenting part when manual elevation cannot be maintained); (4) start IV tocolysis (nifedipine or terbutaline) if delivery is likely to be delayed. Vaginal delivery is only pursued if the cervix is fully dilated with the head at or below spines. Category-1 caesarean is otherwise definitive. The cord should be kept warm and moist without excessive handling; do not attempt to reposition it above the cervix.
key_points: Manual elevation of presenting part is first-line during transfer.
Bladder filling with 500 mL saline relieves compression when hands must be freed.
Tocolysis buys time if there is any transfer delay.
Category-1 caesarean is definitive unless immediate vaginal delivery is possible.
explanation.pearls: In cord prolapse elevate the presenting part manually, fill the bladder with 500 mL saline, position in knee-chest and give tocolysis; deliver by category-1 caesarean within 30 minutes unless the cervix is fully dilated and head is at or below spines.

options.rationale: Cord replacement is not routine; it risks cord damage and delays delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

Oxytocin worsens compression by contracting uterus; the immediate need is delivery by category-1 caesarean unless immediate vaginal birth is possible. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)
Instrumental delivery requires the head at or below the ischial spines with cervix fully dilated; -2 station at 6 cm is not amenable. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)
Symphysiotomy is not part of the AU cord prolapse pathway; category-1 caesarean is the definitive management. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

RANZCOG cord prolapse pathway uses manual elevation, positioning to relieve compression, bladder filling and tocolysis while transferring urgently to theatre for delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

explanation.summary: In refractory PPH after full pharmacological uterotonic escalation (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol), the RANZCOG pathway moves to mechanical measures - intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri, Rusch or Foley) - with concurrent blood product resuscitation. Massive transfusion protocol should be activated for ongoing losses above 40 percent blood volume with hypotension or coagulopathy; NBA guidance uses 1:1:1 ratios of PRBC, FFP and platelets with early cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L. Warm the patient (hypothermia worsens coagulation). If balloon tamponade fails, surgical options are B-Lynch or other compression sutures, then internal iliac artery ligation or uterine artery embolisation, then hysterectomy as the definitive step. Balancing correction of the four Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) continues throughout.
key_points: After pharmacological failure move to balloon tamponade with continued transfusion.
Activate MTP for >40 percent blood volume loss with hypotension or coagulopathy.
Cryoprecipitate is added early when fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L.
Hysterectomy is the definitive final step if mechanical and other surgical measures fail.
explanation.pearls: After maximal uterotonic therapy fails in PPH, transfer to theatre for intrauterine balloon tamponade with concurrent massive transfusion protocol activation, cryoprecipitate replacement of low fibrinogen, active warming and preparation for surgical compression sutures.

options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH management escalates to mechanical tamponade (Bakri balloon) after pharmacological failure while blood product resuscitation continues; MTP activation covers ongoing coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; National Blood Authority MTP)
Carboprost is capped at 8 doses in total but tone-directed pharmacological therapy has already failed here; mechanical measures are indicated. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
A second TXA dose is given at 30 minutes if bleeding continues, but escalation to mechanical and surgical measures should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
Hysterectomy is definitive but is generally preceded by balloon tamponade or uterine compression sutures; jumping to hysterectomy skips reversible mechanical measures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
Ongoing haemorrhage above 2 litres with hypotension and coagulopathy requires immediate escalation, not observation. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: The ADIPS 75 g OGTT diagnostic thresholds for GDM at 24-28 weeks are fasting 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher. Any single value meets diagnosis. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by fasting 7.0 mmol/L or higher, random 11.1 mmol/L or higher, or HbA1c 6.5 percent or higher and requires immediate specialist input. GDM initial management is lifestyle modification plus 1-2 week trial with self-monitoring targets fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L. If targets not met, metformin or insulin is added; insulin remains the mainstay for tight fasting control.

Any single value exceeding threshold diagnoses GDM.
First-line is diet, exercise and self-monitoring for 1-2 weeks.
Add metformin or insulin if targets not met.
explanation.pearls: ADIPS GDM thresholds on 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L; any one value at threshold diagnoses GDM.

explanation.summary: A previous infant with invasive group B streptococcal disease marks a woman as having a persistently high genital tract load or an infant-level susceptibility, and the recurrence risk in a subsequent pregnancy is high enough that Australian guidance makes intrapartum prophylaxis automatic. She is not swabbed at 35 to 37 weeks, because a negative result would not change the plan and risks misleading the birth suite team. The same override applies to significant group B streptococcal bacteriuria in the index pregnancy. Postnatal debriefing after a neonatal unit admission is also the moment to talk through what happened, to document the standing indication clearly in her record, and to offer psychological support where the admission was distressing. In context, clear documentation is what turns this piece of history into an antibiotic actually given during the next labour.
key_points: A previous infant with invasive disease is a standing indication in every later pregnancy.
No 35 to 37 week swab is needed once that indication exists.
Caesarean section is not a preventive strategy for this infection.
Document the indication prominently so the birth suite team acts on it.
explanation.pearls: Postnatal debriefing after a neonatal unit admission is also a screening opportunity for perinatal anxiety and post-traumatic symptoms, which are common after an unexpected separation from the baby.

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of vaginal birth (1000 mL for caesarean), most commonly from uterine atony. Management combines bimanual compression and bladder emptying, uterotonic escalation, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of onset, and blood product resuscitation. Ergometrine and syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because they trigger hypertensive crisis, so the escalation ladder skips to carboprost intramuscularly. Misoprostol is used where carboprost is unavailable, and refractory bleeding leads to balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation or surgery.
key_points: Ergometrine and syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia.
Carboprost is the appropriate second-line agent after oxytocin in these patients.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be given within 3 hours of onset as adjunct.
Consider balloon tamponade or surgery for refractory bleeding.
explanation.pearls: In postpartum haemorrhage with hypertension or pre-eclampsia, skip ergometrine and syntometrine and escalate directly from oxytocin to carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular.

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive women; carboprost is the appropriate escalation when oxytocin is already running and hypertension precludes ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it precipitates hypertensive crisis. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Syntometrine contains ergometrine and is contraindicated in hypertension for the same reason. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Misoprostol is an option in resource-poor settings; in Australian tertiary units carboprost is preferred second-line for atony refractory to oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Tranexamic acid is a valuable adjunct to uterotonics but does not replace an additional uterotonic when uterine atony continues. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: The aim of tocolysis in preterm labour is to delay delivery by 48 hours so antenatal corticosteroids can act and in-utero transfer can occur if required. Nifedipine is the Australian first-line agent based on efficacy equivalent to atosiban, oral administration, low cost and acceptable side-effect profile. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular is given as two doses 24 hours apart when delivery is anticipated between 24 and 34+6 weeks. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is used at gestations under 30 weeks; indometacin is reserved for gestations under 32 weeks for up to 48 hours.
key_points: Nifedipine is the Australian first-line tocolytic in preterm labour.
Aim is 48 hours delay for antenatal steroid effect and transfer.
Magnesium sulfate is neuroprotective, not tocolytic, and used under 30 weeks.
Indometacin only under 32 weeks and limited to 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: For preterm labour under 34 weeks in Australia, first-line tocolysis is nifedipine 20 mg oral stat then titrated dosing to buy 48 hours for corticosteroid effect.

options.rationale: Beta agonists cause significant maternal cardiovascular side effects and are no longer preferred first-line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)
Nifedipine is the first-line tocolytic in Australian practice with a favourable maternal safety profile and equivalent efficacy to atosiban. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)
Atosiban is effective but is not typically first-line in Australia due to cost; nifedipine is preferred initial choice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)
Indometacin is used only under 32 weeks for limited duration due to premature ductus arteriosus closure risk; nifedipine is broader-use first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)
Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection under 30 weeks but is not effective as a tocolytic; a separate tocolytic is required. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy include beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, no significant pain, reliable follow-up and no contraindications (renal or hepatic dysfunction, blood dyscrasia, breastfeeding, active pulmonary or peptic ulcer disease, immunodeficiency). Salpingectomy is preferred when the contralateral tube is healthy because recurrence risk after salpingostomy in the same tube is higher than a new ectopic in a normal contralateral tube. However, when the contralateral tube has already been removed or is grossly diseased, salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility. Methotrexate is an alternative when surgery is declined but has a longer resolution timeline and lower success in the setting.
key_points: Salpingectomy is preferred when contralateral tube is healthy.
Salpingostomy is preferred when contralateral tube is absent or diseased.
Methotrexate requires beta hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm and no cardiac activity.
Direct sac injection is reserved for cornual or interstitial ectopics.
explanation.pearls: Prior contralateral salpingectomy inverts the usual salpingectomy-vs-salpingostomy preference: preserve the only remaining tube with salpingostomy where technically feasible.

options.rationale: Expectant management requires falling beta hCG and small mass; her beta hCG is rising which excludes this pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

Methotrexate is a reasonable option (mass under 3.5 cm, beta hCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, no significant pain), but with the contralateral tube already lost, preserving fertility takes priority; conservative surgical salpingostomy is preferred over medical management here to allow future ipsilateral tubal function without waiting weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

With prior contralateral salpingectomy the right tube is her only tube; conservative salpingostomy preserves tubal patency while removing the ectopic and gives the best chance of future spontaneous conception. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

Salpingectomy on the sole remaining tube commits her to IVF; salpingostomy preserves tubal function and is preferred if technically feasible in this context. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)
Direct sac injection is used for cornual or interstitial ectopic; standard tubal ectopic is managed medically with systemic methotrexate or surgically. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with end-organ dysfunction (renal impairment, hepatic derangement, thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L, cerebral or visual disturbance, pulmonary oedema) at less than 34 weeks gestation warrants stabilisation, magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroid administration and planned delivery within 24-48 hours, provided fetal and maternal condition allow. Immediate delivery is indicated for eclampsia, uncontrollable hypertension despite maximal therapy, pulmonary oedema, non-reassuring fetal status, or placental abruption. Blood pressure target during labour is under 160/110 mmHg. Fluid restriction (80 mL/h) is preferred over aggressive resuscitation because of the risk of pulmonary oedema. Magnesium is continued for 24 hours post-delivery.
key_points: Delivery is definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia.
Severe pre-eclampsia at less than 34 weeks: steroid, stabilise, deliver in 24-48 hours.
Fluid restrict to 80 mL/h; avoid aggressive volume loading.
Continue magnesium for 24 hours post-delivery.
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia under 34 weeks with end-organ involvement, deliver within 24-48 hours after antenatal corticosteroid; do not push fluids for oliguria as pulmonary oedema is the greater risk.

options.rationale: She has severe pre-eclampsia with end-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, haematologic); delaying delivery risks eclampsia, HELLP progression and abruption. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Australian NCSP uses a primary HPV screening approach with reflex cytology on positive samples. Higher risk (HPV 16 or 18 detected, or intermediate risk with any HSIL cytology) triggers direct colposcopy referral. Intermediate risk (oncogenic HPV non-16/18 with negative, unsatisfactory, or low-grade cytology) triggers repeat HPV test in 12 months, with colposcopy if oncogenic HPV persists. Lower risk (HPV negative) returns to 5-yearly screening. Immediate colposcopy also applies to symptomatic bleeding, visible cervical lesion, or clinical suspicion regardless of screen result.
key_points: HPV 16 or 18 detected: refer to colposcopy.
Non-16/18 with HSIL cytology: refer to colposcopy.
Non-16/18 with normal or low-grade cytology: repeat in 12 months.
Symptomatic bleeding or visible lesion: refer regardless of result.
explanation.pearls: Under the National Cervical Screening Program, non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with normal or low-grade cytology is intermediate risk: repeat HPV in 12 months.

options.rationale: The 6-month follow-up applies to unsatisfactory or borderline categories; this is intermediate risk requiring 12-month HPV. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

pLSIL with non-16/18 HPV is intermediate risk in the NCSP; direct colposcopy referral is triggered by HSIL, HPV 16 or 18, or symptomatic bleeding, not intermediate risk. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)
LLETZ is reserved for confirmed high-grade lesions at colposcopy; low-grade lesions are surveilled, not excised. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)
Vaccinated women still require screening as scheduled; a positive HPV result mandates the standard risk-stratified follow-up regardless of vaccination. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)
Non-16/18 HPV with negative or low-grade cytology is intermediate risk in the NCSP; 12-month HPV recall is the standard pathway. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture during VBAC is uncommon (0.3-0.7 percent) but catastrophic. Signs include abnormal cardiotocography (bradycardia in around 70 percent of cases is the earliest sign), maternal haemodynamic instability, severe suprapubic pain breaking through epidural, PV bleeding, loss of station of the presenting part, and cessation of previously effective contractions. Immediate management is cessation of oxytocin and category 1 caesarean section; delay increases perinatal and maternal mortality. Repair of the uterus at laparotomy may be possible but hysterectomy is required if bleeding cannot be controlled. Oxytocin augmentation in VBAC labour is associated with increased rupture risk and requires careful titration.
key_points: Loss of station plus tearing pain plus maternal shock is diagnostic of rupture.
Fetal bradycardia is the earliest and commonest CTG finding.
Cease oxytocin immediately and proceed to category 1 caesarean.
Oxytocin augmentation increases rupture risk in VBAC.
explanation.pearls: In VBAC labour, sudden loss of station of the presenting part with tearing pain breaking through the epidural and maternal shock is uterine rupture; call the category 1 caesarean immediately.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.rationale: This clinical picture is diagnostic of uterine rupture; category 1 caesarean is the only life-saving intervention for mother and fetus. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)

options.rationale: Masking pain from uterine rupture and continuing labour risks maternal exsanguination and fetal death. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse after artificial rupture of membranes requires immediate action to relieve compression while a Category 1 caesarean is arranged. The examining hand elevates the presenting part off the cord and remains in situ until delivery. The mother is placed in knee-chest or steep left lateral Trendelenburg, and bladder filling with 500 to 700 mL of warm saline via an indwelling catheter reduces cord pressure. Tocolysis with subcutaneous terbutaline 250 micrograms can be used if there is contraction-related deceleration and delivery is delayed. Cord handling should be minimised to avoid vasospasm; if the cord is outside the introitus, replace it gently in the vagina. Delivery within 30 minutes of diagnosis is targeted.
key_points: Elevate the presenting part with the examining hand and keep it there.
Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg reduces gravitational cord pressure.
Bladder filling with warm saline further offloads the cord.
Tocolysis with terbutaline is the adjunct if delivery is delayed.
explanation.pearls: After ARM-triggered cord prolapse, keep the examining hand elevating the presenting part, position knee-chest and fill the bladder with warm saline while theatre is prepared for Category 1 caesarean.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Obstetric emergencies - Cord prolapse

options.rationale: Instrumental or spontaneous vaginal delivery is only appropriate when the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low; at 5 cm dilatation vaginal birth is not achievable. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)
Ergometrine causes uterine hyperstimulation and is contraindicated with a live fetus in utero; it would worsen fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)
Cutting the cord terminates fetal circulation and is only ever considered after delivery; it must never be done with a live fetus in utero. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

Elevating the presenting part off the cord, gravity positioning and bladder filling all reduce cord compression while theatre is prepared for Category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

Oxytocin augmentation increases contractions and cord compression; tocolysis (e.g. terbutaline) is the correct pharmacological adjunct while awaiting theatre. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Universal antenatal culture-based screening for group B streptococcus is the AU standard between 35 and 37 weeks. Screen-positive women receive intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, ideally starting at least 4 hours before delivery. First-line is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g 4-hourly. In non-severe penicillin allergy (rash without anaphylaxis) IV cefazolin is used. In documented anaphylaxis, treatment depends on isolate sensitivity: IV clindamycin if the isolate is confirmed clindamycin-sensitive, otherwise IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) 8-hourly. Empirical clindamycin is discouraged because resistance rates approach 20 percent. Neonatal observation is guided by mother's antibiotic duration and neonatal risk factors, not a substitute for prophylaxis.
key_points: First-line intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g then 1.8 g 4-hourly.
Cefazolin for non-severe penicillin allergy; vancomycin for anaphylaxis without known clindamycin sensitivity.
Empirical clindamycin is discouraged due to ~20 percent resistance.
Effective prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours before delivery.
explanation.pearls: In labouring GBS-positive women with prior penicillin anaphylaxis and unknown clindamycin susceptibility, give IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours until delivery.

explanation.summary: Active management of the third stage of labour combines a prophylactic uterotonic, controlled cord traction and uterine massage. In Australia, IM oxytocin 10 units is the standard uterotonic and is given with delivery of the anterior shoulder or immediately after birth. Syntometrine (ergometrine 500 micrograms plus oxytocin 5 units) offers slightly lower blood loss but is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders because ergometrine can precipitate stroke. Misoprostol 600 to 800 micrograms is reserved for settings without cold-chain access to oxytocin. Delayed cord clamping of 1 to 3 minutes is compatible with active management and is standard practice. Women with prior PPH remain candidates for standard active management with a lower threshold for early uterotonic escalation.
key_points: IM oxytocin 10 units is the standard AU prophylactic uterotonic.
Syntometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Misoprostol is second-line where oxytocin is unavailable.
Delayed cord clamping is compatible with active management.
explanation.pearls: In a labouring woman with gestational hypertension, use IM oxytocin 10 units for third-stage prophylaxis rather than Syntometrine, which contains ergometrine and is contraindicated.

explanation.summary: Surgical management of tubal ectopic pregnancy in Australia is laparoscopy first-line. The choice between salpingectomy (removing the affected tube) and salpingostomy (opening the tube and evacuating the ectopic) is guided by contralateral tube status and future fertility plans. When the contralateral tube is normal, salpingectomy is preferred because salpingostomy leaves 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast requiring further intervention and does not improve future spontaneous conception rates. When the contralateral tube has already been removed (prior salpingectomy), the affected tube is the last remaining tube - salpingectomy is still preferred because recurrence risk in a compromised tube is high, and IVF becomes the fertility plan. Methotrexate is contraindicated when there is fetal cardiac activity, beta-hCG above 5000 IU/L, mass over 3.5 cm, significant pain or haemorrhage.
key_points: Laparoscopy is first-line surgical management for tubal ectopic.
Salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy when tube function is impaired or contralateral tube absent.
Methotrexate contraindicated with cardiac activity or beta-hCG above 5000 IU/L.
IVF is the fertility plan after bilateral salpingectomy.
explanation.pearls: In tubal ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy, salpingectomy of the last remaining tube plus IVF outperforms salpingostomy for cumulative reproductive success.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: With prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; salpingostomy carries a 5 to 15 percent risk of persistent trophoblast plus higher recurrence in the same tube, both worse than salpingectomy plus IVF for future fertility. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: After a prior contralateral salpingectomy the affected side is the only remaining tube; salpingectomy avoids persistent trophoblast and recurrence risk, and IVF is the fertility plan given loss of tubes. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Methotrexate is contraindicated when there is fetal cardiac activity or beta-hCG above 5000 IU/L per RANZCOG criteria; both apply here. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) can present or worsen postpartum in up to 30 percent of cases. Diagnostic criteria include microangiopathic haemolysis (fragments on film, LDH above 600 U/L, low haptoglobin), AST or ALT above twice normal, and platelets below 100 x10^9/L. Presentation may lack antenatal hypertension. Treatment is the same as for antenatal severe pre-eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g per hour for seizure prophylaxis, rapid antihypertensive control (labetalol IV 20 mg boluses, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine per SOMANZ), fluid restriction to avoid pulmonary oedema, and close monitoring for hepatic haematoma or DIC. Steroids and platelet transfusion are not routine unless bleeding or platelets below 20 x10^9/L for delivery.
key_points: Postpartum HELLP can present without antenatal hypertension.
Diagnostic triad: haemolysis, transaminase elevation, thrombocytopenia.
Treat with magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour plus rapid antihypertensive.
Steroids not routine; platelet transfusion only for active bleeding or under 20.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum HELLP without antecedent hypertension needs magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour plus IV labetalol; steroids and imaging come later.

options.rationale: Sepsis is a differential but the haematology, liver enzymes, hypertension, hyperreflexia and proteinuria are classic for postpartum HELLP; empirical antibiotics alone will not address the underlying pathology. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
Uterus is contracted with normal lochia; there is no active haemorrhage and ergometrine is contraindicated with severe hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Postpartum HELLP with severe range hypertension and hyperreflexia needs magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and rapid antihypertensive control; both are SOMANZ first-line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Delaying treatment for imaging in a woman with severe postpartum hypertension and hyperreflexia risks eclampsia and stroke; treat first, image second. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Steroid therapy for HELLP has not been shown to improve maternal outcomes and is not part of the SOMANZ pathway; magnesium and blood pressure control are the immediate priorities. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption is a clinical diagnosis in a woman with painful bleeding, a tender woody uterus, fetal compromise on cardiotocography and features of coagulopathy. Bleeding may be revealed or concealed, and haemodynamic status can be worse than the visible loss suggests. Ultrasound has poor sensitivity and should not delay treatment. In contrast, placenta praevia typically presents with painless bleeding and a soft non-tender uterus. When abruption is complicated by coagulopathy and fetal compromise, immediate delivery (usually Category 1 caesarean unless the fetus is already dead and the mother is stable) is required, with activation of the massive transfusion protocol, correction of fibrinogen to at least 2.0 g/L using fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate, and early involvement of anaesthesia and haematology.
key_points: Painful bleeding with tender woody uterus and coagulopathy is abruption.
Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption; do not delay delivery.
Correct fibrinogen to at least 2.0 g/L with concentrate or cryoprecipitate.
Category 1 caesarean when fetal compromise and coagulopathy coexist.
explanation.pearls: In painful antepartum bleeding with a woody uterus, fetal late decelerations and fibrinogen below 2 g/L, activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to Category 1 caesarean without waiting for ultrasound.

options.rationale: The clinical picture is diagnostic for concealed abruption with disseminated intravascular coagulation and fetal compromise; delaying delivery for ultrasound is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption with coagulopathy and fetal compromise; delivery must proceed and antenatal steroids are given but do not delay delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Late decelerations with reduced variability plus concealed abruption already indicate significant fetal compromise; delay increases perinatal mortality. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Concealed abruption with hypovolaemia, DIC and fetal compromise mandates activation of MTP, coagulopathy correction and immediate operative delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is only given if delivery can be delayed by at least 4 hours; here delivery must be immediate. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) presents with sudden peripartum cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and disseminated intravascular coagulation, often during or immediately after delivery. It is a clinical diagnosis; there is no confirmatory test acutely. Echocardiographic findings of a dilated dyskinetic right ventricle with septal bowing help distinguish AFE from primary obstetric haemorrhage (in which the right ventricle looks empty). Management is high-quality CPR per ANZCOR, perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes if there is no return of maternal circulation, activation of the massive transfusion protocol, correction of fibrinogen to at least 2 g/L (fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate), inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (e.g. nitric oxide) and inotrope support for right ventricular failure, and consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in tertiary centres. Recovery is possible but maternal and neonatal mortality remain high.
key_points: AFE is a clinical diagnosis; treat empirically on the picture.
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes if no ROSC.
Correct fibrinogen to at least 2 g/L with concentrate or cryoprecipitate.
RV failure: inhaled pulmonary vasodilator plus inotrope; consider ECMO.
explanation.pearls: In peripartum arrest with pink frothy secretions, DIC and dyskinetic right ventricle on point-of-care echocardiography, treat as amniotic fluid embolism with perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes, MTP with fibrinogen concentrate, and pulmonary vasodilator support.

options.rationale: The picture of sudden collapse during crowning with rapid coagulopathy and DIC is amniotic fluid embolism; thrombolysis would worsen the obstetric haemorrhage and is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)
ANZCOR adrenaline dose in adult arrest is 1 mg (not 5 mg) every 3 to 5 minutes; 5 mg is not evidence-based and risks tachyarrhythmia. (Source: ANZCOR ALS Adult)
Line insertion is important but does not take priority over perimortem caesarean and coagulopathy correction, and adds no immediate treatment in this crisis. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)
ANZCOR mandates perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes of arrest in a viable pregnancy; deferring until ROSC forgoes the aortocaval decompression that facilitates return. (Source: ANZCOR ALS Adult)

AFE with cardiovascular collapse and DIC needs perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes, coagulopathy correction with fibrinogen concentrate, and pulmonary vasodilator plus inotrope support for the dyskinetic right ventricle. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)
